name: eager-acquisition
intent: Acquire and initialise a resource before anything needs it - at construction, at process start-up or at task activation - so every use pays a small, predictable cost and any acquisition failure surfaces before the deadline instead of inside it.
problem: A resource whose acquisition is slow, blocking or failure-prone - a connection, a decoded model, a thread pool, a buffer, a warm cache - is first touched on a path that has a deadline: the first call pays the whole cost, the latency curve shows unexplained spikes after every cold start, and a misconfigured dependency is discovered inside a user request rather than during deployment. The recurring decision is whether to acquire the resource up front and hold it, or to keep deferring its cost to first use.
context: Applies wherever the use-time budget is tight or contractual (real-time and control loops, latency-SLO services, media and trading paths, batch windows) and start-up is a controlled phase that may perform I/O while the hot path may not. It is a resource-lifecycle policy of the resource's owner rather than of a call site: it also applies inside an object that pre-warms its own dependencies during construction, and inside a worker that provisions everything before entering its loop.
benefits: Use-time cost becomes predictable: no acquisition, pool growth, decoding or class loading happens on the critical path, so first-use latency stops dominating the tail after every cold start.

Failures surface where they are cheapest to handle - a dependency that is down, unreachable or misconfigured stops the start-up or fails the readiness check, instead of failing an arbitrary later request.
The contention burst at the first request disappears: pre-started workers, pre-filled pools and pre-built indexes let the system run at steady-state cost from the first unit of traffic.
Acquisition logic exists once, in one controlled initialisation path, instead of being duplicated - or accidentally omitted - at every use site.
Deadline-bearing systems become feasible at all: a hard real-time or contractual deadline can only be met when allocation, connection setup and decoding are paid outside it.
Start-up work becomes measurable and governable: the eager set is an explicit, observable budget with a readiness gate instead of an invisible tax spread over the first minutes of traffic.
tradeoffs: The cost moves to start-up, the phase where it is often most expensive: serverless cold starts, autoscaling latency, CLI invocation time and rolling-deploy windows all get worse.

Resources acquired for code paths that are never taken sit idle while paying memory, file descriptors, connection slots or licences - an eagerly filled pool for a rarely used dependency is pure overhead.

Boot becomes dependency-coupled: an unavailable dependency can prevent the process from starting at all, and when the acquisition runs inside a once/static-initialisation construct the failure is cached for the process lifetime (a type-initialisation error on the JVM and in .NET, a panic in init() in Go), turning a partial outage into a total one.

Idle resources rot: connections and leases are reaped by NAT, firewall, load-balancer and database idle timeouts before their first use, so eager acquisition without validation converts a lazy failure into a stale one.

The eager set is a policy that must be maintained: as dependencies, traffic patterns and deployment topology change, an unmaintained eager set either over-provisions at boot or quietly recreates the cold-path problem it was meant to remove.

Tests and local development pay the full warm-up unless the acquisition seam is injectable, and the initialisation path is a second code path with its own failure policy, timeouts and observability to design.

participants.responsibility: The thing whose acquisition is moved earlier: a connection, session, buffer, worker thread, file handle, decoded model or warm cache entry - it has a non-trivial creation cost and a lifetime somebody has to own.

Supplies and validates the resource: an allocator, pool, connection factory, runtime or loader. It may itself need preparation (pool construction, credentials, transport bootstrap) before the resource can be handed out.
Performs the acquisition before use and owns the resource for its lifetime - usually the component that will consume it (a service, an instance, a worker) or a dedicated lifecycle manager.

The hook that makes the acquisition early: a constructor, a static/type initializer, an init()/main bootstrap, an application factory, a host start-up callback or a readiness gate. It runs once, inside a controlled phase, and must be idempotent.

Code whose budget must be met. It reads an already-acquired resource and pays no acquisition cost, and it depends on the Acquisition Point having completed - signalled by readiness, health or explicit sequencing.

use_cases: Service bootstrap: open and pre-fill the database pool, load configuration and secrets, build TLS contexts and pre-touch hot caches before the readiness probe starts routing traffic.
Latency-critical first call: trading, telecom and media paths where a lazy model load or cache warm-up would blow the deadline - decode the model and build the lookup tables at boot.
Worker capacity: pre-start executor threads (prestartAllCoreThreads, a pre-spawned goroutine pool) so the first burst does not pay thread-creation and scheduler latency.
Real-time and embedded loops: pre-allocate buffers, DMA-capable memory and fixed-size queues during initialisation so the control loop contains no allocation or blocking call.
Batch and ETL windows: open every shard, file and index before the processing window starts, so the whole window is productive instead of paying setup.
Cold-start-sensitive deployments: provisioned concurrency, warmed container pools or an explicit warm-up endpoint after a deploy, moving JIT and first-call cost out of user traffic.
Cache warm-up in front of a hot read path: populate the entries the next minutes of traffic will ask for, so the source of truth never sees a miss storm at start-up.
HTTP client pool hardening: configure pool_max_idle_per_host and pool_idle_timeout with tcp_keepalive on long-running services to prevent silent connection rot after hours of idle time.
Database connection pool validation: validate connections on checkout (e.g., Hibernate's validate() or HikariCP's connectionTestQuery) rather than trusting the pool to be healthy after idle periods.

Microservice dependency pre-warming: eagerly resolve service mesh certificates, feature flag values and remote configuration before accepting traffic, so a cold dependency does not cascade into a request failure.
ML model serving: load and compile the inference model during the initialization phase of the serving process, keeping the handler path pure computation.

Serverless function initialization: move heavy library imports, JIT compilation and one-time setup into the init phase (Lambda's init handler, Provisioned Concurrency environments) so the handler stays lean.

Spring container boot: ApplicationContext pre-instantiates all non-lazy singleton beans at context refresh by default, so misconfiguration, missing dependencies and bad credentials fail the boot instead of the first request; @Lazy exists precisely to opt rarely used beans out of the eager set.

PostgreSQL pg_prewarm: preload relation blocks into the OS or shared buffer cache at server start; the autoprewarm worker records the cached block set and reloads it after a restart so the first queries post-restart skip cold disk reads.

Kubernetes pod bootstrap: init containers run setup work - waiting for dependencies, preloading data, fetching configuration - sequentially to completion before any app container starts, so the app container's first action already finds its resources in place.
avoid_when: The resource may never be needed and the process is short-lived (one-shot CLI, migration script, serverless handler with long idle gaps): use lazy acquisition or lazy initialization and pay on first use.
Start-up time is the scarce resource (serverless cold start, aggressive autoscaling, fast rollbacks): keep acquisition lazy and warm up in the background rather than blocking readiness.
The resource is expensive, shared and used rarely: pool it (object-pool) or split it so only the cheap part is eager (partial-acquisition) instead of giving every owner its own eager copy.

The resource is idle-timeout-prone and cannot be validated cheaply: acquire lazily, or keep the eager pool alive with keepalive/validation, instead of holding a stale connection for hours to save milliseconds.
A non-critical dependency would take the whole process down at boot: apply graceful degradation or a fail-fast boundary and acquire eagerly only what the process genuinely cannot serve without.

An infrastructure layer already warms it (platform-managed connection pools, DI container eager singletons, pre-warmed container pools): configure that mechanism instead of writing a second acquisition path.
anti_patterns: Acquiring everything eagerly 'just in case': boot time, memory and file descriptors balloon for resources most executions never touch - the pattern applied as a reflex instead of a measured decision.

Eager acquisition without validation: the pool is filled and the handles are open, and the first request discovers that the credentials expired or that a middlebox reaped the idle connection long ago.

Hiding a design problem behind warm-up: preloading a huge dataset or pre-computing a response because the use site was never made proportional - the cost is not removed, only moved where it is harder to see.

Performing I/O or taking locks inside a language-level once/static-initialisation construct, where the failure gets cached (or a deadlock with the initialisation lock is created) and the ordering against other initialisers is unspecified.

Eagerly provisioning more than the system can serve - hundreds of idle pool connections or worker threads at boot - so the process exhausts its own memory, its file descriptors or the dependency's connection limit before it serves anyone.

Treating eager acquisition as a substitute for a health signal: warm resources are not proven working resources, and a readiness probe that flips healthy before the acquisition has finished routes traffic straight into the cold path.

Leaving idle connections unvalidated: not configuring pool_idle_timeout or TCP keepalive on long-running HTTP clients, so connections go stale and produce silent failures (200 OK with empty body) after hours of inactivity.

Eager acquisition inside a constructor that is called from another constructor or from a parent-class constructor before the object is fully initialized, leaking a reference to a not-yet-constructed object to another thread.
design_principles: Keep the deadline-bearing path free of acquisition: move provisioning, allocation and decoding out of the hot path into a controlled phase.
Fail fast at start-up: detect dependency failure where handling is cheapest - before traffic, not inside a user request.
Explicit resource ownership and lifecycle: the owner acquires, validates and releases, so acquisition policy belongs to the owner rather than to each call site.
Make the cost visible and budgeted: start-up work is measured and bounded, and readiness depends on its completion.
Separation of concerns: provisioning is separated from use, and the acquisition point stays idempotent with no surprise side effects.
Validate before trusting: construction success is not proof of usability - prove the resource works with a canary call or health check.

Deterministic release: pair every eager acquisition with a corresponding release (RAII destructor, Dispose, context manager __exit__) so resources are not leaked on any code path including exceptions.
best_practices: Acquire eagerly only for resources that are on the critical path or certain to be used; keep the rest lazy, and measure before turning the policy on.
Bound the eager phase: acquisition timeouts, a start-up budget and an explicit failure policy (fail the boot, degrade, or retry with backoff) - never let one dependency hang start-up indefinitely.
Validate rather than merely construct: open and ping a connection, decode the model, make a canary call; successful construction is not proof of usability.
Gate readiness - or acceptance of traffic - on completion of the eager phase, and report progress so slow start-ups stay diagnosable.
Keep idle resources fresh: pool keepalive/validation and recycle intervals shorter than the infrastructure's idle timeout, or acquire lazily where that cannot be guaranteed.
Make acquisition injectable and skippable so tests and local runs bootstrap cheaply, and idempotent so a warm-up hook can replay it after a deploy.
Pair the eager phase with deterministic release (RAII, Dispose, execute-around) and re-evaluate the eager set whenever the dependency or deployment topology changes.
Pre-start core thread pool threads (e.g., ThreadPoolExecutor.prestartAllCoreThreads()) before the first task arrives to eliminate thread-creation latency from the hot path.

Configure connection pool idle timeouts and TCP keepalive to match infrastructure limits (firewall, NAT, load-balancer) - connections left idle longer than the timeout are silently reaped, turning eager acquisition into a stale-resource problem.

In cloud/serverless environments, use provisioned concurrency or pre-warmed containers, but keep the initialization phase outside the handler and validate resources with a health probe before routing traffic.

For language-level static/once initializers (Go init(), Java static blocks, C# static constructors), move fallible I/O out of them into explicit initialization methods that return errors - cached init failures are process-lifetime failures.
Use sync.Once or equivalent in Go to replace fallible init() calls, enabling proper error propagation and test isolation.
